To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the reduction of diphenylphosphoryl‐β‐haloalkyl esters 3a‐e in the presence of the mercury electrode leads to diphenylphosphate.
the reduction of the diphenylphosphoryl halide esters is a two‐step process.
the reduction of diphenylphosphoryl halides 3a - c at the mercury electrode in the presence of water leads to the formation of the corresponding phosphoric acid 4a - c and the halide anion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the electrochemical reduction of diphenylphosphoryl esters of the type 3, in which the phosphoryl group is bonded to an alkyl chain containing a halogen atom in the 3 position.
the development of new, selective and efficient methods for the synthesis of organic compounds.
the electrochemical reduction of diphenylphosphoric acid esters of the general structure 3a - d in order to obtain diphenylphosphate 4 and the electrochemical reduction potential of these esters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the electrochemical behavior of the title compounds is strongly dependent on the halide and on the presence of geminal halogen atoms.
the electroreductive cleavage of β‐halogenated diphenylphosphates 3a – e at the Hg‐electrode proceeds via the formation of a radical anion, followed by an E1CB‐type reaction.
the reduction of the title compounds 3a-e at the mercury electrode leads to the corresponding phosphoric acid derivatives 1a-e.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the electrochemical reduction of diphenylphosphoryl halides leads to the formation of phosphates, if no other reactions take place, e. g. reduction of the halogen substituents.
the electrochemical reduction of diphenylphosphorus acid esters 3a -e at the mercury electrode gives diphenylphosphate 4a.
we have shown that electrochemical methods can be successfully used for the synthesis of phosphorus containing compounds and that these methods are superior to chemical methods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a single‐electron‐transfer‐mediator (SET‐mediator) is a promising strategy to improve the performance of electrocatalytic water oxidation catalysts (WOCs) in neutral electrolytes.
we have shown the first example of a phosphorus‐based electrochemical protection group that is capable of protecting a ketone from reduction.
we can use electrochemistry to selectively reduce a variety of diphenylphosphoryl esters to their phosphoric acid derivatives.
